summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Customer needs cost predictability for a high-volume summarization pipeline, exploring batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization options. Important stakeholders: ML, Platform, and Finance. Next steps: pricing sheet, benchmark plan, and sample data for perf runs.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42m
Attendees: Julia Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Aster Head of ML), Priya Nair (Aster Platform), Leo Martin (Aster CFO)

[00:00] Julia Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Julia, AE at Redwood. Samir is our SE, he'll dig into perf and cost.
[00:12] Michael Chen: Hi Julia, hi Samir — thanks, I'm Michael. We handle a lot of large-doc summarization and want to understand cost per token and where Dedicated or Private makes sense.
[00:20] Leo Martin: Leo here, CFO — I'll be focused on TCO and budget impact.
[00:27] Priya Nair: And Priya from platform, I'll own networking/SLA side.
[00:33] Samir Patel: Great, quick agenda: 1) current infra + token volumes, 2) cost levers (batching, caching, quant), 3) Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, 4) next steps.
[01:05] Michael: Quick context — prod pipeline ingests ~1.5M documents per week, average doc 2.2k tokens, peak concurrency around 600 reqs/min. Right now we use a mix of third-party APIs and some self-hosted models for experiments.
[01:28] Leo: Our monthly token budget target is around $120k - that's allocated across embeddings + generation. We need predictability.
[01:40] Julia: Understood. On Hosted we price per-token; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU throughput which lowers unit cost once you commit, and Private is for strict compliance or data residency with higher fixed costs.
[01:58] Michael: Can you quantify — ballpark unit costs for hosted vs dedicated?
[02:05] Samir: For a generation model roughly comparable to Llama2-13B, Hosted list might be $0.0003 - $0.0005 per token depending on model and decoder params; Dedicated can drop to ~$0.00012 - $0.0002 per token once you amortize reserved capacity and leverage batching/caching. Private on-prem is variable — higher infra ops + licensing, but per-token compute cost can be close to Dedicated if you have spare GPU capacity.
[02:32] Priya: Those ranges are wide; what are main drivers of the difference?
[02:36] Samir: Two big buckets: 1) fixed capacity costs (reserved GPUs) vs pay-as-you-go; 2) runtime efficiency — batching and KV/prefix caching reduce per-token GPU work. Also quantization — int8/4-bit profiles reduce memory and increase throughput.
[03:05] Michael: We do a lot of long-context summarization; KV cache reuse should help. How much caching helps for long docs?
[03:12] Samir: If your requests are sequential and reuse prefixes, KV caching can cut token compute by 20-60% depending on reuse patterns. For example, for multi-chunk summarization where you repeatedly query the same base context, caching saves recomputation. We'll need your actual prompt sequences to estimate.
[03:35] Michael: We'll share sample prompt set.
[03:38] Leo: On Dedicated commits — how predictable is throughput? If we reserve X cards, can we guarantee 600 reqs/min at p95 latency?
[03:47] Samir: Yes, Dedicated includes configurable autoscale and throughput profiles. We provide performance SLOs and usage dashboards. We size an initial cluster by modeling your token distribution, concurrency, and latency target. There are headroom/burst options for spikes.
[04:10] Priya: Network: with Private we need VPC peering and no egress to public internet. Does Redwood Private support air-gapped options?
[04:18] Julia: Yes, we offer Private deployments with customer-managed networking and on-prem packages for air-gapped environments; that typically pushes cost up due to ops and support.
[04:27] Michael: One of our concerns is variability in per-token cost because of different prompt lengths and model choices — can Redwood provide a modeled TCO spreadsheet?
[04:36] Julia: Absolutely, we'll send a TCO model that takes token distribution, batching rates, caching hit rates, and reserved capacity to compute unit cost.
[04:45] Samir: A few important knobs: batching window — bigger windows increase throughput but add latency; continuous batching and dynamic batching in Redwood can be tuned per-route. Also prefix caching and memoization — if you can accept slightly higher tail latency during cache misses, overall CPU/GPU spend drops.
[05:12] Michael: What's the typical batching window in production? We're latency sensitive — p95 under 700ms.
[05:18] Samir: For strict p95 under 700ms we'll target small batching windows (10-25ms) and rely on KV caching to reduce load; that still gives some batching benefits. For non-interactive background jobs you can use larger windows and get much better amortization.
[05:40] Priya: How does Redwood measure token counts? We need alignment with our finance team — tokens measured at model input+output? Any normalization differences?
[05:49] Julia: We report tokens as model-processed tokens (input + output). We'll share the exact tokenizer mapping per model for reconciliation.
[05:58] Leo: Regarding discounts — are there volume tiers or committed discounts on hosted?
[06:03] Julia: Hosted has tiered pricing and committed volume discounts. Dedicated is effectively a reservation model with lower marginal unit costs in exchange for a monthly capacity fee. We'll detail numbers in the pricing sheet.
[06:18] Michael: On model variants — you mentioned fallback to cheaper variants when capacity constrained. How does quality regression get monitored?
[06:26] Samir: We have evaluation hooks and quality monitoring tied to prompt sets and can alert on regressions. For production you can define a fallback policy (e.g., model-v1 -> model-v1-quant -> model-v0.9) and Redwood will route with regen or A/B testing.
[06:50] Michael: For our use, accuracy is important; we can't accept big regressions to save cost. So dedicated looks attractive if it offers both lower cost and consistent model choice.
[06:59] Samir: Exactly — Dedicated reduces variability and supports pinning exact model binaries.
[07:10] Priya: Security: we need SOC2 Type II, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs for every inference request. Does Redwood provide per-request audit and KMS?
[07:19] Julia: Yes — Redwood offers SOC2, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations. Private gives you full control over keys if needed. We'll attach our security pack.
[07:29] Leo: For Private, what are the fixed costs we should model? Hardware provisioning, software license, support and deployment. Can Redwood help with initial sizing?
[07:38] Samir: We help with sizing and offer a managed install option. Fixed costs include cluster provisioning, on-prem ops, and often a consulting/setup fee. We'll include those in the TCO.
[07:52] Michael: Walk me through an example calculation — say 100M tokens/day generation workload, average response 200 tokens. Rough math?
[07:59] Samir: Quick rough: 100M tokens/day -> ~3B tokens/month. On Hosted at $0.00035/token avg -> $1.05M/month. On Dedicated with reserved fleet and 40% batching/caching effective reduction and lower base unit cost maybe $0.00015 -> $450k/month plus reservation fee. These are illustrative; real numbers depend on batching hit rates and model architecture.
[08:29] Leo: That's a big delta. Can we run a benchmark to validate cost assumptions?
[08:34] Julia: Yes, Samir will run a bench with your sample prompts on our Hosted or Dedicated staging depending on access. We'll need token distribution and some representative concurrency.
[08:43] Michael: We'll share sample prompts and production token histogram.
[08:47] Priya: On SLAs, what uptime and latency commitments come with Dedicated?
[08:52] Julia: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; exact terms depend on committed capacity and region. We'll include SLA language in the next email.
[09:05] Leo: For finance approval we'd like a 12-month forecast with sensitivity to caching hit-rates (0%, 25%, 50%) and to batching windows. Can Redwood TCO model support that?
[09:14] Julia: Yes, the TCO model will include parameters for cache hit, batching factor, and model mix so you can run scenarios.
[09:22] Samir: Also consider quantization — some workloads tolerate int8/4-bit with minimal quality loss yielding 1.5-2x throughput improvements. That reflects in the TCO.
[09:36] Michael: Any caveats on quantization for summarization? We rely on nuanced output — not sure about 4-bit.
[09:41] Samir: It's workload dependent. We recommend running evals on your prompt set; often int8 is safe, 4-bit sometimes needs validation. We'll include quality regressions benchmarks.
[09:56] Priya: Network egress costs: if we run Private in our VPC, do you still have egress? We prefer no public egress for data protection.
[10:03] Julia: Private can be fully VPC-contained with no public egress — that is a common configuration for regulated customers.
[10:12] Michael: On monitoring: does Redwood provide token-level cost dashboards and per-route breakdowns?
[10:16] Samir: Yes — Console gives token-level cost breakdowns, route/model heatmaps, and tracing. That helps teams identify expensive prompts.
[10:27] Leo: For our approval we also want competitor benchmarks — where does Redwood typically win versus OpenAI hosted?
[10:34] Julia: In Hosted, model choice and price competitiveness vary; Redwood emphasizes predictable performance, batching/caching controls, and dedicated capacity which often yields better unit economics at scale compared to pure pay-as-you-go public endpoints. We'll add comparative notes.
[10:50] Michael: Ok practical steps — what do you need from us to run a tailored cost model?
[10:55] Samir: Token histogram (by percentile), average response token sizes, concurrency patterns, latency SLO targets, and a sample prompt/test harness. Also preferred region and any compliance constraints.
[11:08] Michael: We'll provide that.
[11:12] Priya: About timeline, if we want a pilot on Dedicated, how long to spin up a test cluster?
[11:18] Samir: Typically 2-4 weeks for reserved cluster provisioning and integration, shorter for Hosted tests. Private on-prem takes longer depending on procurement.
[11:27] Leo: Pricing cadence: once you send pricing, can you show committed vs pay-as-you-go breakeven point? We want to know at what token volume Dedicated becomes cheaper.
[11:37] Julia: Yes, the TCO will show a breakeven analysis and sensitivity curves.
[11:44] Michael: A couple of specific technical Qs: 1) do you support dynamic model quantization and automated kernel selection? 2) is KV cache persisted across requests or ephemeral?
[11:55] Samir: We support quantization profiles and runtime kernel selection based on model and hardware. KV cache is typically per-inference session but Redwood also supports longer-lived prefix caching patterns via cache keys, so you can persist reusable context between related requests.
[12:16] Michael: That would really help our summarization flow.
[12:19] Samir: We'll sketch out how you'd key cache entries (conversation id, doc id, chunk index) in the benchmark plan.
[12:28] Priya: Any vendor lock concerns with Dedicated or Private? We need ability to export models and configs.
[12:33] Julia: You can pin models and export model artifacts; Private gives the most control. We avoid lock-in by supporting open model binaries and standard deployment formats.
[12:46] Leo: On billing — can you provide daily cost reporting to our finance system?
[12:50] Julia: Yes, we support detailed usage exports and can integrate with billing hooks or S3 exports.
[13:00] Michael: Great. For the bench, can we run both Hosted and Dedicated back-to-back to compare latency/cost?
[13:06] Samir: Yes. For Hosted we'll use equivalent model family; for Dedicated we'll provision a staging fleet sized for your concurrency. We'll measure tokens/sec, p50/p95 latencies, and cost per million tokens given measured batching/caching.
[13:22] Priya: We need to ensure keys and data handling for sample prompts — can Redwood sign an NDA or data processing addendum?
[13:29] Julia: Yes, we'll share DPA/NDA templates.
[13:34] Michael: Anything else we should know about unexpected hidden costs?
[13:38] Samir: Watch for network egress on multi-region deployments, storage for large context caching, and the management overhead for Private on-prem. We'll flag those in the TCO.
[13:52] Leo: Sounds good.
[13:54] Julia: Quick recap — Aster to share token histograms, sample prompts, and concurrency patterns; Redwood to send pricing + TCO model, security pack, and benchmark plan. We'll schedule benchmark the week of 3/9.
[14:10] Michael: Confirmed. Thanks all.
[14:15] Priya: Thanks.
[14:18] Leo: Thanks, bye.

Notes: transcription has occasional mis-hearings (e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash); speaker turns sometimes merged. Links referenced: Pricing sheet (link to be sent), Security pack (SOC2 doc link), Benchmark plan template (to be shared).
